clinicalPearls: This group spans endemic dimorphic fungi (paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis, adiaspiromycosis), hyaline and dematiaceous molds (fusariosis, scedosporiosis/lomentosporiosis, phaeohyphomycoses), and the yeast-like Trichosporon; the more common invasive mycoses (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, candidiasis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis) are covered separately (Harrison 22e p.1725).

Dimorphic fungi exist as conidia-producing molds in the environment (the infectious form) and convert to yeast (or spherules/adiaspores) at temperatures above about 35 degrees C in tissue; infection generally begins with inhalation of conidia (Harrison 22e p.1725).

Paracoccidioidomycosis (Paracoccidioides brasiliensis complex, P. lutzii) is acquired by inhalation in humid Central/South American forests, with highest incidence in Brazil; chronic disease shows a striking male predominance (reported male-to-female ratios from 14:1 up to ~70:1) (Harrison 22e p.1726).

The acute/juvenile form of paracoccidioidomycosis is uncommon, occurs typically in those under 30, primarily disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system, and often shows peripheral eosinophilia; the chronic/adult form accounts for ~90% of cases (Harrison 22e p.1726).

On tissue, Paracoccidioides yeast classically appears as a central yeast ringed by narrow-necked daughter buds (the 'mariner's wheel'); some commercial serologic tests may fail to detect P. lutzii (Harrison 22e p.1726).

Talaromycosis (Talaromyces marneffei, formerly Penicillium marneffei) is endemic in Vietnam, Thailand, and other Southeast Asian countries, is epidemiologically linked to bamboo rats, and occurs mostly in advanced AIDS; its presentation mimics disseminated histoplasmosis with umbilicated molluscum-like skin papules (Harrison 22e p.1727).

In culture T. marneffei produces a distinctive diffusible red pigment, and tissue/blood smears show yeast-like organisms reproducing by bipolar fission (two ellipses with a central septum) (Harrison 22e p.1727).

Emergomycosis (Emergomyces, several formerly Emmonsia) is an emerging dimorphic-fungus infection of patients with impaired cellular immunity; cutaneous involvement (disseminated ulcers, papules, nodules) accompanies pulmonary disease in most patients, while CNS spread is rare (Harrison 22e p.1727).

Fusariosis is angioinvasive and mimics aspergillosis, but is distinguished by very common, often painful, nodular or necrotic skin lesions appearing around the onset of fever and by frequently positive blood cultures (~50%); banana-shaped macroconidia are characteristic on culture (Harrison 22e p.1728).

Phaeohyphomycoses are caused by melanin-producing (dematiaceous/brown-black) molds; melanin is a virulence factor, certain species (Cladophialophora bantiana, Rhinocladiella mackenziei) are neurotropic, and golden-brown hyphae are highlighted by the Fontana-Masson melanin stain (Harrison 22e p.1728).

Trichosporonosis (most often Trichosporon asahii) resembles invasive candidiasis with fungemia, but the presence of arthroconidia helps distinguish it from candidemia, and the serum cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test can be falsely positive because T. asahii shares polysaccharide antigens with Cryptococcus neoformans (Harrison 22e p.1729).

Scedosporiosis (Scedosporium apiospermum complex) and lomentosporiosis (Lomentospora prolificans) mimic aspergillosis radiographically and histologically; L. prolificans can grow in blood cultures whereas S. apiospermum usually does not (Harrison 22e p.1729).
harrison.pathophysiology: Most of these fungi enter through inhalation of environmental conidia, with a smaller number introduced by traumatic skin or corneal inoculation or by injection of contaminated material. Dimorphic fungi (Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces, Emergomyces, Emmonsia crescens) convert from mold to invasive yeast/adiaspore form under thermal pressure in the lungs and then disseminate hematogenously to the reticuloendothelial system and other organs; granulomatous inflammation is typical. Disease frequently reflects host immune deficits: inborn errors affecting the IL-12/IFN-gamma axis predispose to severe paracoccidioidomycosis and talaromycosis, and IFN-gamma-primed monocytes/macrophages and neutrophils control Talaromyces. Molds such as Fusarium, Scedosporium, and Lomentospora are angioinvasive, and protection against Fusarium and Trichosporon depends heavily on neutrophils and their oxidative burst, explaining the strong link with profound prolonged neutropenia and with chronic granulomatous disease (defective NADPH oxidase). Dematiaceous molds use melanin as a virulence factor; defense against disseminated phaeohyphomycosis involves Dectin-1 (CLEC7A) and the adaptor CARD9, and deficiencies in this pathway predispose to disseminated and brain infection even in otherwise immunocompetent hosts. In adiaspiromycosis, inhaled E. crescens conidia enlarge into nonreplicating thick-walled adiaspores (up to ~500 micrometers) that drive a granulomatous inflammatory response.
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated histoplasmosis (talaromycosis and emergomycosis mimic it clinically and the Histoplasma antigen test cross-reacts with Emergomyces)
Invasive aspergillosis (fusariosis, scedosporiosis, and lomentosporiosis mimic it clinically, radiographically, and histologically)
Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and squamous cell carcinoma (mimic the mucocutaneous lesions of chronic paracoccidioidomycosis)
Molluscum contagiosum (umbilicated skin papules of talaromycosis)
nonInfectiousMimics: Squamous cell carcinoma (mucocutaneous lesions of paracoccidioidomycosis; rarely arises in chronic chromoblastomycosis)
Necrotic/embolic skin lesions of other causes (mimicked by painful necrotic lesions of fusariosis)
additionalInvestigations: Culture from blood and/or tissue is central; identification to mold phase is often required because yeast/hyphal tissue forms can be misidentified (e.g., Emergomyces resembling Histoplasma; Fusarium/Scedosporium resembling Aspergillus)
Histopathology with special stains, including Fontana-Masson for melanized (dematiaceous) molds
Blood cultures (positive in up to ~50% of disseminated fusariosis and can grow Lomentospora prolificans; S. apiospermum usually negative)
Serology for Paracoccidioides (with the caveat that some assays miss P. lutzii)
PCR-based molecular identification (including 28S rDNA and rRNA ITS) through fungal reference laboratories, useful in culture-negative or difficult cases
Awareness of cross-reactivity: Histoplasma antigen test cross-reacts with Emergomyces; cryptococcal antigen can be positive in Trichosporon asahii infection
Species-level identification and susceptibility testing in a reference laboratory to guide management of resistant molds
redFlags: Persistent fever in a profoundly neutropenic patient despite broad-spectrum antibiotics (suggests angioinvasive mold such as Fusarium or Scedosporium/Lomentospora)
New painful nodular or necrotic skin lesions in a neutropenic or leukemic patient, especially appearing with the onset of fever (fusariosis)
Positive fungal blood culture in an immunocompromised host (disseminated fusariosis or Lomentospora)
Disseminated cutaneous ulcers/papules/nodules with pulmonary disease in an HIV/AIDS or transplant patient (emergomycosis, talaromycosis)
Indolent brain abscess with golden-brown pigmented hyphae, or intraventricular CNS spread (neurotropic dematiaceous molds such as Cladophialophora bantiana)
CNS involvement in any of these disseminated infections, which carries notably high mortality
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by organism and host immune status. Paracoccidioidomycosis generally responds well, though pulmonary fibrosis can progress in chronic disease. Untreated disseminated talaromycosis is usually fatal, but treated mortality is about 10%. Disseminated fusariosis carries high mortality (historically up to ~85%, now around 50% with better therapy) and approaches 100% if neutropenia persists; survival hinges on neutrophil recovery. Invasive S. apiospermum infection has roughly 50% mortality, whereas L. prolificans remains about 85-100% lethal. Disseminated trichosporonosis mortality has been as high as 70% and remains very high with persistent neutropenia. Disseminated and visceral phaeohyphomycoses, particularly with CNS involvement, have high mortality.
pitfalls: Misidentifying tissue forms: Emergomyces can be mistaken for Histoplasma, and Fusarium/Scedosporium/Lomentospora are difficult to distinguish from Aspergillus on histology, so culture identification is essential
Cross-reacting antigen tests can mislead: Histoplasma antigen cross-reacts with Emergomyces, and cryptococcal antigen may be positive in Trichosporon asahii infection
Assuming AmB activity is universal: many of these molds (Scedosporium, Lomentospora) are intrinsically resistant to amphotericin B, and Fusarium MICs are relatively high
Treating a respiratory mold isolate as disease without evidence of tissue invasion, since Scedosporium/Lomentospora may merely colonize the airway (e.g., in bronchiectasis)
In vitro susceptibility of dematiaceous molds may not reflect response because muriform/tissue forms can behave differently from hyphal forms
Overlooking Fusarium onychomycosis as a portal for later disseminated disease in patients heading into neutropenia or transplantation
Missing the diagnosis in 'immunocompetent' patients with disseminated/brain phaeohyphomycosis who may carry CLEC7A/CARD9 pathway defects
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal staging applies across this heterogeneous group. Practically, infections are stratified by extent and host status: localized cutaneous/keratitis/onychomycosis or pulmonary-limited disease versus disseminated/angioinvasive infection; presence of CNS involvement marks the most severe end (associated with the highest mortality). For dimorphic fungi (e.g., paracoccidioidomycosis, talaromycosis, emergomycosis), disease is broadly described as mild/moderate versus severe, and as acute (juvenile) versus chronic (adult) forms for paracoccidioidomycosis.
management: Organism-directed antifungal therapy, typically liposomal amphotericin B for severe disseminated dimorphic-fungal disease followed by an azole such as itraconazole, and voriconazole for fusariosis and scedosporiosis
Recognition that Lomentospora prolificans is frequently multidrug-resistant, often requiring combination antifungal therapy and expert guidance
Restoration of host immunity, including antiretroviral therapy for talaromycosis in advanced AIDS and reversal of neutropenia with growth factors where relevant
Surgical debridement or source control for localised angioinvasive mould disease
Secondary antifungal prophylaxis in patients with ongoing immunosuppression to prevent relapse
Monitoring of cultures, antigen assays and clinical response, with awareness of cross-reactivity in serological tests
Specialist infectious diseases and mycology reference laboratory involvement to confirm species and tailor therapy
